title: The deploy 'succeeded' and production is running an image called shop:null
intro:
A deploy pipeline went green ten minutes ago and the shop pods are now in ImagePullBackOff, trying to pull registry.example.com/shop:null. The deploy script, deploy.sh, asks the release service for the current release and sets the image from its tag. The release service was upgraded yesterday. The script's key lines are:
    TAG=$(curl -s https://releases.internal/api/shop/current | jq -r '.tag')
    kubectl set image deployment/shop shop=registry.example.com/shop:$TAG -n shop

steps.prompt: Stop the damage first. Roll the deployment shop in namespace shop back to its previous revision.
expected_commands: kubectl rollout undo deployment shop -n shop

steps.prompt: Now find the cause. Run the script's own lookup by hand: fetch the current release and extract .tag as raw text.
jq printed the word null: there's no .tag in the response. Look at what the API returns now: show the whole response.
Yesterday's upgrade wrapped the response in a 'data' object, so the tag is at .data.tag. Confirm the corrected lookup, and this time make jq fail if the value is missing.
The path is fixed in deploy.sh. But why did the pipeline go green with a null tag? Check how the script handles errors: show its first 3 lines.

No 'set -euo pipefail': the script keeps going after any failure. What should the script do to make this class of bug impossible?
  a) Retry the deploy three times
  b) Start with set -euo pipefail, use curl -f and jq -e so a bad response fails the pipeline, and check the tag looks like a version before using it
  c) Print the tag at the end
  d) Run the script as root
Type the letter.
steps.hint: Every step that can produce a bad value should be able to fail the script.

resolution: A field moved, and four separate things that should have stopped the deploy each let it through. jq treats a missing key as null and exits 0, and -r prints null as the four letters n-u-l-l, which is a perfectly good string to a shell. The script had no 'set -e', so it would have continued even after a real failure. Nothing checked that the value looked like a version. And the script ended with 'kubectl set image', which succeeds as soon as the API server accepts the change, long before any pod tries to pull the image; so the pipeline reported success while production was rolling out an image that doesn't exist. Kubernetes limited the damage: the rolling update couldn't bring up new pods, so the old ones kept serving. A deployment strategy that had replaced them first would have been an outage. Rolling back took one command and came first, before any diagnosis. The repaired script closes each gap. 'set -euo pipefail' makes any failed command, any unset variable, and any failed stage of a pipe stop the script. 'curl -f' turns an HTTP error into a failure instead of an error page fed to jq. 'jq -e' exits non-zero when the result is null. A pattern check refuses anything that isn't a version. And 'kubectl rollout status' with a timeout makes the pipeline wait for the rollout to actually finish, so green means deployed. The upstream cause deserves a word too: the release service changed its response shape with no version in the URL and no notice. An API that other teams' automation depends on needs a contract (cicd-tutorial-020), and its consumers need tests that run against it.
